energy.overview: Private capital in this layer is split across three maturity tiers: molten-salt and sodium-cooled SMR developers (Kairos Power, TerraPower, Terrestrial Energy, Elementl Power) still in first-of-a-kind construction or permitting; fusion developers (Helion, Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Type One Energy, newcomer Inertia Enterprises) racing toward net-energy or first-power milestones; and long-duration/thermal storage firms (Form Energy, Antora Energy, Fourth Power) that have just crossed from pilot to first commercial-scale deployment.

cooling.overview: The private cooling landscape now splits into direct-to-chip cold plate/CDU specialists (increasingly split between mature single-phase and emerging two-phase/microfluidic approaches), immersion cooling providers (single-phase more commercially proven than two-phase), and specialist air/hybrid integrators serving custom high-density retrofits. Many of the earlier independent leaders have already been folded into public strategics (CoolIT into Ecolab, LiquidStack into Trane, Boyd into Eaton, JetCool into Flex), leaving a next wave of venture-backed independents racing to scale and prove hyperscaler-grade reliability before further consolidation.

power.overview: Private-company activity in this layer splits between grid-flexible/demand-response software that squeezes more capacity out of existing infrastructure (Emerald AI, Verrus, Amperon), non-lithium long-life storage aimed at data center backup and grid buffering (EnerVenue), and fabless backside/vertical power-delivery silicon aimed directly at the AI rack (AmberSemi). The flexibility-software approach is now commercial-scale with utility partnerships live, while the storage and silicon bets are earlier-stage, still ramping first commercial production lines.

silicon.overview: Private companies in this layer split into three distinct bets: alternative AI-compute architectures (Groq, Tenstorrent, SambaNova) that depend entirely on foundry allocation rather than owning fabs and are increasingly pivoting toward cloud/inference services; optical interconnect and co-packaged-optics startups (Ayar Labs, Lightmatter, Celestial AI) racing to commercialize technology that ranges from early customer integration to full acquisition by incumbents; and supply-chain diversification plays — a state-backed alternative foundry (Rapidus) and specialized packaging/equipment vendors (Deca Technologies, ZEISS SMT) — trying to loosen TSMC's and the Korean memory duopoly's grip on the leading edge.

compute.overview: Private compute challengers split into distinct bets: purpose-built inference silicon paired with a neocloud business model (Groq, SambaNova), alternative full-stack architectures competing on RISC-V/chiplet design (Tenstorrent), pure GPU-rental neoclouds riding Nvidia allocation rather than designing chips (Lambda), and analog/in-memory compute aiming at radically higher efficiency for edge inference (EnCharge AI) — with maturity ranging from Lambda's imminent IPO-track scale to EnCharge's still-early client shipments.

networking.overview: Private capital in networking is split between co-packaged optics/optical chiplet startups racing to prove volume manufacturability, and a smaller cohort of alternative compute plays adjacent to networking (quantum control chips, inference silicon) still finding their commercial footing. CPO is the most mature private bet, with Ayar Labs and Lightmatter both shipping samples and forming OEM/rack partnerships, while Celestial AI's exit via Marvell acquisition signals the segment is already consolidating around larger strategic buyers.

serversdc.overview: The operator layer is split between long-established hyperscale campus builders now weighing public listings, enterprise colocation platforms consolidating under private-equity ownership, and a newer wave of cross-border M&A pulling national champions into global AI-infrastructure consortiums. Capital availability is no longer the constraint for most of these players; power, permitting and community acceptance increasingly are.

cloud.overview: Private neoclouds split between vertically integrated, energy-first builders like Crusoe that co-develop power and compute, GPU-rental specialists like Lambda that lean on asset-backed debt to fund hyperscale customer commitments, and newer alternative-silicon or sovereign-focused entrants like Groq and Nscale; nearly all are racing toward an IPO to access cheaper public capital before the financing cycle tightens further.

applications.overview: Private frontier labs are racing on two fronts — raw model capability (GPT-6, Claude Fable/Mythos 5.1, Grok 4.6) and enterprise-grade safety/governance wrappers — while both OpenAI and Anthropic simultaneously prepare public listings that could reset how the whole category is valued. Beneath them, vertical enterprise AI (Harvey in legal, Glean in enterprise search) is proving out real, fast-scaling ARR, and consumer-facing players (Perplexity, Midjourney) are pushing into on-device/hybrid compute and new product categories to defend against commoditized chat interfaces.
